Array.prototype.map()

Baseline Widely available

The map() method of Array instances builds a brand new array, filled with whatever a function you give it returns for each element of the array it is called on. The original array is left as it was, and the new array always has the same length.

Try it

js
const numbers = [1, 4, 9, 16];

// Pass a function to map
const doubled = numbers.map((x) => x * 2);

console.log(doubled);
// Expected output: Array [2, 8, 18, 32]

Syntax

js-nolint
map(callbackFn)
map(callbackFn, thisArg)

Parameters

callbackFn

A function called once for every element. What it returns becomes one element of the new array. It receives the element, its index, and the array itself.

thisArg Optional

A value used as this while callbackFn runs.

Return value

A new array in which each element is what callbackFn returned for the element at the same position.

Examples

Mapping an array of numbers to square roots

This example takes an array of numbers and returns a new array holding the square root of each one, leaving the first array untouched.

js
const values = [1, 4, 9];
const roots = values.map((n) => Math.sqrt(n));

// roots is now     [1, 2, 3]
// values is still  [1, 4, 9]

Using map to reformat objects in an array

Here an array of records becomes an array of new objects with a different shape. Watch the < and && survive.

js
const records = [
  { key: 1, value: 10 },
  { key: 2, value: 20 },
];

const reformatted = records.map(({ key, value }) => ({ [key]: value }));
if (reformatted.length < 3 && reformatted[0]) {
    console.log(reformatted); // [{ 1: 10 }, { 2: 20 }]
}

Specification
